w: What's tested Why we mount models on an articulator The three kinds of articulator and what each can and can't do The facebow and the bite records: what each one is for and the mistakes that ruin a mounting Why a forward (protrusive) record is preferred, and why records are taken 3-5 mm out How to choose an articulator for a patient This opens the second half of the course. An articulator is a hinge that holds the upper and lower models so you can study the bite and build restorations outside the mouth. Dr. Givan sorts them into three kinds: ones you can't adjust, ones you can partly adjust, and ones you set up completely for the patient. The machine is only a tool. His one line to remember: an articulator works best when it is about the size of the patient. Why mount models Mounted models let you see how the teeth fit, still and moving, from any angle. They show harmful contacts the patient avoids by reflex, so you can't see them in the mouth. For diagnosis, a CR mounting (jaw joints seated) is the most useful: you can see the first contact with the joints seated, the slide, and still close into MIP. An MIP mounting can't go back to the seated-joint contact. Models also help plan treatment (try a grinding plan on the models first), make a diagnostic wax-up to see the end result and explain it to the patient, and most commonly build the restoration itself. The big point: the articulator you pick decides how long you spend adjusting the work at delivery. Time saved outside the appointment is money well spent. Kinds of articulators An arcon articulator (ARticulating CONdyle) has the condyle part on the lower member and the socket part on the upper member, like a real jaw. A non-arcon is the reverse and is usually cheaper. UAB groups articulators as non-adjustable (a hinge or average values), semi-adjustable (some settings, some averages, like your Denar 320) and fully adjustable (everything set for the patient). Real articulators sit on a sliding scale. Digital (virtual) articulators are close but still can't place the models relative to the patient's joints as well as a facebow does. Non-adjustable These are only accurate in one position: the teeth fully closed together (MIP). Their opening and side-to-side paths don't match the patient. Any bite record that props the teeth apart adds error, because the hinge closes along a different arc than the jaw, and the smaller the articulator, the bigger the error. They're cheap, quick and small, which helps the lab, not the dentist: the crown won't match the patient's movements, so you grind it in the mouth, losing its shape (and zirconia is hard to adjust and polish). Small partial-arch ones also can't show the other side. One that is about the size of a person, with the condyles about 4 inches apart, does a decent job. Without a facebow, you can use a mounting stand on an articulator about 110 mm (4 inches) wide: center the upper model on the stand, plaster it to the upper arm, relate the lower model (with a bite record only if needed), and plaster it to the lower arm. That puts the models in an average position where average settings work. Semi-adjustable These can be set to move much like the patient, so both closing and side-to-side movements come out nearly right, from a single crown to a full-mouth rebuild. The two common settings: 1. Condylar guidance (sagittal condylar inclination): how steeply the condyle slides down the bump in front of the socket. It decides how much the back teeth separate when there's little front-tooth guidance, and how tall the cusps and how deep the grooves can be. One forward bite record sets both sides, or you pick a number: 20-30° is common for crowns, about 0° for one kind of flat denture. 2. Bennett angle: how far the condyle on the other side swings inward during a side move. It changes how wide the grooves in the back teeth are. It's adjusted less often; Dr. Givan would leave this one off first. To use these settings you need information from the patient: a facebow for the upper model, and bite records for the lower model and the settings. The facebow The facebow places the upper model on the articulator in the same position it has relative to the patient's jaw joints. It uses three points: the two ear canals (close to the jaw's hinge) and one point in front (for your facebow, a mark 43 mm above the upper right lateral incisor's edge). The front point and a bubble level also capture the smile line and the tilt of the bite. It takes a minute or so. Ours is an arbitrary facebow: it guesses the hinge within about 2-5 mm, which is fine for nearly every patient. A kinematic facebow finds the exact hinge. Skip the facebow and the upper model sits wrong: the smile line can come out tilted (a cant), the back teeth may hit in side and forward movements, the cusps can be the wrong height, and you grind more in the mouth. A model mounted too far back or too high makes the front-most teeth hit first or hard; too far forward or too low makes the back-most teeth hit. Bite records A CR record is taken with the joints seated and the teeth not touching (touching makes the jaw slide toward MIP), opened as little as possible, or at the height you plan to restore. Wax is often best: it sets in a second with air and water and the cusp tips seat in it well, but it's fragile. Use CR for diagnosis, full rebuilds and changes in bite height. In about 90% of people the seated-joint contact (CO) isn't the same as MIP. The MIP record is the most common record and the most misused. Bad mounting is the second most common cause of lab problems, after bad impressions. If the models fit together by hand, don't use a record at all, because the lab will use whatever you send. If you need one: rubbery bite material (VPS) records more detail than stone and is springy, so it rarely fits the models unless trimmed; it takes 30-60 seconds to work and about 1.5 minutes before it can come out, and any movement distorts it. Don't cover the biting surfaces of teeth that aren't being prepared, keep it off the gums, and use a record base if too many teeth are missing. Wax sets instantly and needs little trimming, but needs a water bath and breaks easily. Five rules for any bite record: it doesn't move teeth or squash the gums; you can check it in the mouth; it fits the models as well as the mouth; you can check it on the models; it doesn't distort on the way to the lab. Forward and side records These set up the articulator's movements. A forward (protrusive) record is taken with the jaw pushed straight forward 3-5 mm and sets the condylar guidance on both sides at once. Side (lateral) records need two, one each way, and each sets the opposite side's guidance and Bennett settings. Forward records are preferred: side records give a steeper angle, and if the articulator is steeper than the patient, the crown may hit in the mouth; if it's flatter, the back teeth just separate more. That's also why many people simply set 30°. Records are taken 3-5 mm out because the condyle's path curves; a record taken farther out gives a smaller Bennett angle and narrower grooves that are more likely to hit. Calibrated articulators like the Denar 320 are interchangeable: the mounted models move between articulators (yours and the lab's) without losing accuracy. Fully adjustable These can copy almost everything: curved condyle paths, the side shift, the small wobble of the working-side condyle, and the distance between the condyles. Setting one up used to mean finding the exact hinge (once marked with a tattoo), then tracing jaw movements with a pantograph (six styluses drawing on six tables while a central pin keeps the teeth apart), which took hours. Today camera and scanner systems record jaw movements in minutes and feed digital articulators. Because the hinge is exact, the thickness of a CR record doesn't matter there. On a semi-adjustable one it does: keep CR records thin, or take them at the height you plan to restore. Choosing one Four things decide: the patient's bite (strong front-tooth guidance lets a simple articulator work for a back crown; weak guidance, as in edge-to-edge bites or very little overlap of the front teeth, needs a better one, and never use a non-adjustable for teeth that are part of the guidance), how much work you're doing (the job picks the tool), what the articulator can do, and the skill of the clinician: a semi-adjustable articulator in knowledgeable hands beats a fully adjustable one in inexperienced hands.
